bol.role: Senior Frontend Engineer (Loyalty and Digital teams)

body.paragraph: bol.com is one of the largest online retailers in the Netherlands and Belgium. Its storefront ran on a large Java application that is being replaced by a server-side-rendered React platform. Since July 2025 I have been the frontend specialist there in teams made up mostly of backend developers, first in Loyalty and then in Digital. The engagement has been extended three times.

The pages I had to move had no written specification. Their behaviour lived in server-side Java and 226 Handlebars templates. I read that code and wrote down what each page actually does: the exact URLs, the user-facing text, the classification rules and the analytics events. I checked my reading with the backend engineers who own the services. That blueprint is what made a low-risk, page-by-page migration possible.
body.heading: The specification that did not exist

body.paragraph: In Loyalty I built the Select points-overview page from that specification to production. It carries a rewards table for order points and action points, Dutch and French text, and edge cases such as cancelled orders and external merchants. In Digital I built the shared page where a customer manages both a Kobo Plus and a Select subscription. The server fetches both subscriptions at once and one pure function maps the result to one of five mutually exclusive situations, so every situation is derived in one place. Where the schema did not fit a data-driven frontend, I took the change into the GraphQL contract with the backend team. One example is a bare mandate reference that became a structured mandate object.
body.heading: Loyalty and the shared subscription page

body.paragraph: I rebuilt the Kobo Plus acquisition page as a server-rendered page whose content marketers manage in the headless CMS. One page registry swaps the seasonal, experiment and refer-a-friend variants with a single line of code, and visitors who arrive through an invitation see a personalised hero. Marketing has been changing that page ever since without an engineering deploy.
body.heading: Marketing without a deploy

body.paragraph: In Digital I built the app for software and games from an empty folder to production inside the Nx monorepo. That included server rendering, routing, CI/CD, Google Cloud and Kubernetes, the security profile and the authentication allow-list. I then ran the cut-over of the live account pages through the platform's routing layer, which another team owns. Employees saw the new pages first, then a percentage of customers, hashed per visitor so nobody bounced between the old and the new page. Every step was reversible in one move. During the ramp I found and fixed a route-matching-order bug. Customers moved across with no customer-facing outage.
body.heading: The Digital app and the cut-over

body.paragraph: With the designer and the business team I shipped nine A/B experiments across five places in the shop, from the acquisition page to the product page and the basket. I built them in code and configured them in the experimentation tool. Winning variants delivered GMV uplifts of up to 24% (roughly 5% to 24% across the winners). Not every experiment won, so the aggregate effect was positive but modest. When a variant won I made it the new default and removed the experiment scaffolding.
body.heading: Nine experiments

body.paragraph: I also made the numbers behind those decisions trustworthy. Placeholder identifiers became real product IDs, so the product-page and basket funnels line up again. I rewrote an all-or-nothing GraphQL handler, so a partial response still shows what is there while every error reaches Sentry. I switched Sentry on end-to-end with readable stack traces on staging and production. For the Kobo Plus promotion codes every backend outcome got its own message, so a customer never sees a generic error.
body.heading: Numbers that hold up

body.paragraph: Almost every change touched code owned by another team. I coordinated with two teams continuously, and with up to six at once for larger features and production issues. In refinement I ask a lot of questions, so edge cases surface early and estimates hold up. I mentored junior developers and reviewed the work of fellow seniors, usually by pulling someone into a conversation about the feature so we arrived at the best solution together. GraphQL stayed the contract between frontend and backend, and I wrote backend logic in Kotlin when capacity was tight.
body.heading: Working across team boundaries

body.paragraph: What I hand over has to be maintainable by a team whose strength is the backend. The components are typed and small, the types run from the GraphQL query into the component without casts, responsibilities stay separate, and every page carries unit tests, GraphQL mocks and a Storybook story per scenario. Accessibility follows WCAG 2.2 AA. While building I kept raising design flaws and possible improvements with the product owner and the designer. Those conversations happened while there was still room to act on them.
body.heading: What stays behind

body.paragraph: The Belastingdienst publishes tax pages and forms that entrepreneurs across the country have to be able to use. A new page in the entrepreneur portal took one to two weeks of frontend work. A new income-tax form took months, with a constant stream of questions running between the content editors and the development team. My assignment was to make that faster without giving up accessibility or consistency. The engagement was extended four times.

For the entrepreneur portal I designed a data-driven Angular architecture in which pages are assembled from backend configuration. Generic components take their logic and their appearance from injectable services and configuration files, so the VAT page, the payroll-tax page and the flight-tax page share the same building blocks. Conditional visibility, multilingual labels and validation rules come from JSON schemas. I added the filter set with dropdowns, search fields and removable chips. A wrapper sorts small tables in the browser according to column type and the sorting rules of the Bold design system.
body.heading: Pages from configuration

body.paragraph: That approach became the foundation under the visual forms editor I then built from scratch. Editors drag form blocks onto a canvas and configure each block in a side panel: labels, validations, conditions and dependencies, with comments and versions per component. In a tryout view they run their own form the way a visitor sees it. I worked on the backend as well and extended the endpoints. The editors' work is stored in configuration files, so the state of every form is reproducible from the backend.
body.heading: The visual forms editor

body.paragraph: The back-and-forth with the development team is gone. In the entrepreneur portal a new page went from one to two weeks to one to two days. Both stayed at WCAG 2.1 AA, verified with automated tests in the pipeline.
body.heading: From weeks to days

body.paragraph: The Bold design system, built as Stencil Web Components, only pays off once other teams actually use it. I worked hands-on with developers across multiple teams on their implementation. I wrote wrappers and documentation so the components behave predictably in Angular, React and Vue. I sat down with Product Owners to unblock them and speed up their rollout. I also tutored a senior developer who knew JavaScript and Vue but no Angular. I took him by the hand through RxJS and streams, which was the hardest part for him, and through the proper use of services.
body.heading: The design system in the teams

body.paragraph: What stayed behind is a platform other developers can keep working in. The code reads without a guide, responsibilities are not tangled together, unit tests cover the logic, and the technical documentation in Confluence carries per-framework examples, edge cases and limitations. CI/CD ran through GitLab, Jenkins, Tekton and ArgoCD, with test automation in Cypress and Playwright. While building I put design flaws and possible improvements to the product owner and the designer, so they were resolved in the design and not repaired in the code.
body.heading: What stays behind

body.paragraph: The lotteries live on campaigns. Every campaign got its own site, and every site was built up again from the start. That took weeks, and the result differed per brand. There was nothing to build on yet, so the design system started from zero.

I built an international design system in an Nx monorepo, where a campaign page is assembled from JSON. The components are React with Next.js and render on the server, the content comes from the Storyblok headless CMS, and accessibility to WCAG 2.1 AA sits inside the components themselves. A second layer carries the brand, so colours, buttons and animations change per label while the logic of a component stays the same. The first campaign site proved the approach, and the VriendenLoterij VIP-Kaarten campaign followed on the same components.
body.heading: One component set, a theme per label

body.paragraph: That held across the European labels. Serverless APIs on AWS deliver the dynamic content, and GitLab pipelines and Docker put a campaign live. Playwright and Cypress keep watch over the existing campaigns while new ones arrive.
body.heading: Across the European labels

body.paragraph: I worked the components out with the designers and the marketing teams, and design choices that did not hold up in code I raised while I was building them. What stayed behind is a tested component library the teams build on themselves, and a way of working in which a new label comes down to a theme.

body.paragraph: Athlon ran its self-service application on Angular 1.6. The framework was long past its useful life, the interface was hard to change, and accessibility was not where it had to be. Everything the application already did had to keep working.

I led the migration to Angular 12 and designed the frontend architecture around RxJS and reactive data streams. On top of that I built a component library that gives every screen the same behaviour and the same accessible markup. That library is what kept the rebuild affordable, because each new screen is assembled from parts that were already tested.
body.heading: From Angular 1.6 to 12

body.paragraph: For the customer side I built a generic self-service platform with conditional logic and validation, configurable in the same low-code spirit. The dashboards got dynamic data visualisations with responsive charts and sortable tables. The frontend talks to several backend REST APIs through OpenAPI 3.0, the content comes from a headless CMS, and delivery runs on Azure DevOps with Docker and Kubernetes.
body.heading: Self-service and dashboards

body.paragraph: The application came back on a current stack, accessible to WCAG 2.1 AA and straightforward to extend.

I tutored the developers around me in the best practices of Angular, junior and senior alike, and took them by the hand where the framework got in their way. I did their code reviews and helped them make their code better. With the UX designers I turned wireframes and user feedback into one consistent, accessible frontend. Design flaws that showed up while building went back to the designer and the product owner while there was still room to change them.

body.paragraph: Opinity needed a business-critical record of trips and freight, and there were four months to deliver it. I took on the front end and the backend both to make that work, and made the architectural calls as I went.

The application is Angular at the front and ASP.NET Core behind it, with authentication and role-based access. Drivers enter the truck number, the pickup and delivery location, the weight on departure and on arrival, and the number of packages loaded and unloaded. Managers see those same entries and verify them. Validation sits in the interface and in the API, so a mistake surfaces at the moment someone makes it.
The application went live on time, works on a phone and is built for use out on the road and on site.

body.paragraph: The platform ran on AngularJS with a .NET backend of the same age. Omniplan wanted to work with outside organisations, and that asks for access you can grant per party. The existing setup did not allow it, so the front end and the backend were rebuilt together.

I migrated the front end to Angular 9 and moved the backend to .NET Core with REST and gRPC services. Alongside that I designed a modular authorisation and membership service on Microsoft Identity and JWT, which gives an outside organisation exactly the rights that belong to its role. The services run on Azure App Services with Docker and Kubernetes, and the data model in Entity Framework on MSSQL was laid out again.

The screens take their behaviour from the configuration in the backend. Validations, permissions and input fields became a setting, so a functional change often needs no new front-end code. Connecting a new partner became a matter of configuration.
I left a platform behind in which authorisation is a separate, reusable service. New integrations connect to it while the rest of the system stays as it is.

body.paragraph: Ortec builds planning software for logistics. FedEx wanted that planning visible to the people who run and follow the routes. The data sat spread across .NET Core microservices and kept changing, and that stream had to come together on one screen.

I built the Angular front end of the portal. It carries interactive route and geo visualisations, data tables with sorting and filtering, and forms that point out straight away what does not fit. Updates arrive through observables, so a change in the planning appears on screen without anyone refreshing. Screen behaviour comes from configuration, which lets the same components serve several views. The front end is set up as micro-frontends on top of the .NET Core microservices, so parts can be released on their own.
Deployment ran through Docker to Azure inside a CI/CD pipeline, so a change reached the users without manual steps.

I settled the REST contracts with the backend teams on OpenAPI, which kept the front end and the microservices in step while both sides changed. What stayed behind is a portal that takes new integrations and new views without a rebuild.

body.paragraph: At Bluefield Smart Access I worked for the clients Bluefield served, among them Ziggo and Tommy Hilfiger. The thread through all of it was the same. There was a lot of data, and the people working with it could not see where their attention was needed.

For the cycle dashboard I pulled the data out of a Neo4J graph database and put every cycle on screen as a tile with a status in colour. From a tile a user opens the diagnostics or starts a recovery action. The front end is React with a Redux architecture, the backend a .NET Web API.

For Ziggo I built a WPF application for network administrators and a map view in React on which incidents appear as they happen, with faulty network nodes marked. It reached the C# microservices through an Angular layer, with RabbitMQ and MassTransit carrying the messages. For Tommy Hilfiger I built an application in which employees reserve a parking spot in a calendar and get an access ticket. All of it ran in a Docker pipeline.

body.paragraph: Transdev ran on a Delphi backend that modern web and mobile applications could not reach. Authentication and authorisation sit at application level, so external systems could reach the data in one uniform way.

questions.question: Who are you and what do you do?
questions.answer: I am Hilmar van der Veen, a freelance senior frontend engineer. I rebuild the pages a business earns its money on without taking them offline, and I leave behind a team that ships faster afterwards. I have more than ten years of frontend experience, senior throughout since 2016, in React and Angular. I work through my own company, Hilmar ICT Services, KVK 97564303, based in Zandvoort.

questions.question: When are you available and for how many hours?
questions.answer: From 1 October 2026, and earlier by arrangement. 32 to 40 hours a week, for six months or longer. My current engagement at bol.com started in July 2025 and has been extended three times. On 1 October 2026 bol.com ends the engagement of all external staff, and mine ends with it.

questions.question: Where do you work, and in which languages?
questions.answer: In the Randstad and remote. Amsterdam, Utrecht, Rotterdam and Den Haag are all within reach, and fully remote works too. My preference is hybrid with one to two days a week on site. I work in Dutch and in English. Dutch is my native language and my English is fluent.

questions.question: Which technologies do you work in?
questions.answer: React and Angular are where the depth sits, with TypeScript throughout. Around that: Next.js and React Router for server-side rendering, GraphQL as the contract with the backend, RxJS in Angular, Tailwind and SCSS, Storybook and Nx monorepos. Testing runs on Vitest, Jest, Playwright and Cypress. On the platform side Node, Docker, Kubernetes, GitLab CI and Azure DevOps, on Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. I have also written Kotlin and C# on backend work.

questions.question: What kind of organisations do you work for?
questions.answer: Dutch e-commerce, enterprise and government organisations with a codebase that already carries real traffic. bol.com, the Belastingdienst, the Nationale Postcode Loterij, Athlon, Ortec and Transdev are the recent ones. The work suits teams that already have engineers and want a senior frontend engineer beside them.

questions.question: What are your certifications and education?
questions.answer: BSc Physics and Astronomy at the University of Amsterdam, 2012. Through bol.com I completed the full Certified Secure engineer curriculum: Essential Security, Essential Specialties, Security Specialist, Web Security Specialist and Server Security Specialist. On top of that came hands-on training in secure development, full-stack vulnerabilities and Kubernetes network security. Compliance training covered personal data under the GDPR and the EU AI Act. Accessibility to WCAG 2.1 AA and 2.2 AA is a default in my work.

questions.question: What does the frontend work look like in practice?
questions.answer: I rebuild pages customers use, in React or Angular, and put them live without a stop. At bol.com I moved the Kobo Plus and Select pages off the legacy Java webshop onto React, page by page, and ran the traffic cut-over. Employees first, then a percentage of customers, ramping to everyone, reversible at every step.

questions.question: Do you also build the backend?
questions.answer: When the build needs it, yes. At the Belastingdienst I built the visual forms editor and wrote the backend endpoints it called. At Omniplan I moved a legacy AngularJS and .NET application to Angular 9 with a .NET Core REST and gRPC layer, including a modular service for login and membership. At bol.com I contributed backend logic in Kotlin when capacity was tight. My centre of gravity stays frontend.

questions.question: What do you deliver on a design system?
questions.answer: Design tokens, a component library with variants and states, Storybook as the documentation, and accessibility built into the components. At the Belastingdienst the shared components were Stencil web components used inside Angular, React and Vue. A new page went from one to two weeks to one to two days. At the Nationale Postcode Loterij a JSON-driven design system brought a campaign site down from weeks to a few days across European labels.

questions.question: What does the consulting and coaching cover?
questions.answer: Architecture and code review, a migration plan in reversible steps, and coaching on the team's own tickets. At Athlon I reviewed the frontend team's code and coached junior and senior developers on Angular while the application moved off Angular 1.6. At the Belastingdienst I taught a senior developer who knew JavaScript and Vue how RxJS, streams and services work. At bol.com I reviewed changes that crossed team boundaries, routinely with two teams and with up to six at once.

questions.question: Can you take over a legacy migration?
questions.answer: That is the work I do most. The old system comes first. I read the existing code to work out exactly what a page does, write that behaviour down, rebuild it, and release it behind a switch that ramps by percentage. At bol.com the legacy was a large Java storefront with its own rendering engine and Handlebars templates, and the rebuild went live page by page. At Athlon it was an Angular 1.6 application that moved to Angular 12.

questions.question: Do you work on accessibility?
questions.answer: Yes. Accessibility is part of building a component. WCAG 2.2 AA at bol.com and WCAG 2.1 AA on the earlier engagements, checked while the components are built, with Playwright and Cypress running the checks in the pipeline.

questions.question: How do you keep a page fast?
questions.answer: By measuring on your own pages. I look at what the server renders, how much data a page fetches and which code the browser really needs. Then I take on the part that carries the most traffic first, and we compare the measurement before and after.

questions.question: What is your rate?
questions.answer: €95 to €125 per hour, depending on project type and work, excluding VAT. Where you land inside that range follows from the scope we agree in the call.

questions.question: What will this cost me?
questions.answer: That follows from the scope, and the first call is where the scope gets set. We go through the page or the team, what has to change, and how many hours a week that needs. After the call you get the hours, the rate within the range and the assumptions behind both, in writing.

questions.question: How does invoicing work?
questions.answer: Monthly, on hours worked, from Hilmar ICT Services (KVK 97564303). Hours are recorded per week and shared with whoever approves them on your side. Amounts are excluding VAT.

questions.question: What contract form do you work under?
questions.answer: Freelance only, through my own company Hilmar ICT Services (KVK 97564303), on an assignment contract per engagement. That is the one form I work in.

questions.question: What if the scope changes during the engagement?
questions.answer: Scope moves, and on migration work that is normal. When something new turns up I say what it costs in hours and what it pushes back, before it is picked up. You decide whether it goes in. The rate does not change during the engagement.

questions.question: What happens in the first call?
questions.answer: Thirty minutes, no obligation. You describe the page, the application or the team, and I say what I would do first and how I would scope it. Nothing is invoiced for that conversation.

questions.question: What does the first month look like?
questions.answer: Reading first, then shipping. At bol.com I read the legacy Java pages to work out what they did. Within weeks a page of mine was live in production and I was reviewing merge requests for other teams. Elsewhere it goes the same way. Understand the system, ship something real early, and start reviewing the work around me.

questions.question: How do you put changes live?
questions.answer: Behind a switch, ramped by percentage, and reversible. A change goes live for employees first, then for a slice of customers, with each visitor kept in the same group, then for everyone. One switch sends the traffic back. On the bol.com account pages that ramp surfaced a routing order bug before customers ever saw it.

questions.question: What do you leave behind when the engagement ends?
questions.answer: Unit tests and mocked network responses next to the components, Storybook stories that show the intended usage, and a written handover with a walk-through for the developers who continue. Where a legacy system was involved, the behaviour I extracted from it is written down too, so the next rebuild does not start from zero.

questions.question: How do you communicate during an engagement?
questions.answer: In the team's own rhythm. I join refinement and sprint review and ask a lot of questions there, because that is where hidden edge cases turn up and where estimates get better. When a decision touches design or product, I raise it with the designer and the product owner while the work is happening.

questions.question: How do you handle problems in production?
questions.answer: By making sure they surface. Error monitoring goes on per page with readable stack traces, and a warning that hides a real backend failure gets promoted to an error. At bol.com customers were seeing an empty list because the data layer discarded a whole response whenever any error came back. After the fix the page shows what did arrive and the error still reaches monitoring.

questions.question: Do you work with experiments and measurement?
questions.answer: Yes, when the page is commercial. At bol.com I built nine A/B experiments in code and configured them in the experimentation tool, with the designer and the business team. I also repaired tracking that carried placeholder identifiers, because a funnel is only worth what its data says.

questions.question: How do you handle performance?
questions.answer: Without a percentage up front. I start with what a visitor notices: server-side rendering so the page stands before JavaScript runs, images and fonts sized to fit, and a limit on third-party scripts. Then I measure on your platform, per page and with real visitors, and we discuss what those numbers say. A figure I have not measured on your platform myself is not one I quote.

questions.question: Do you work on site or remote?
questions.answer: Hybrid, with one to two days a week on site in the Randstad, and fully remote works too. Amsterdam, Utrecht, Rotterdam and Den Haag are within reach on the same terms. I am based in Zandvoort and work in the Dutch timezone.

questions.question: Can you work inside our existing team?
questions.answer: That is the normal setup. I join the team's rituals, take tickets from the same board, and review the work around me. At bol.com almost every change I shipped touched another team's area, so merging meant agreeing an approach with the team that owned it. I was in regular contact with two teams and, for larger features or production issues, with up to six at once.

questions.question: How do you work with our backend team?
questions.answer: Through the contract between us. I treat the GraphQL schema, or the shape of the REST API, as an agreement about what the frontend gets. When a field makes the interface awkward, I go back to the backend engineers and we change it at the source. At bol.com that turned a flat reference string into a structured object, which kept the page driven by its data.

questions.question: How do the Dutch DBA rules apply to this?
questions.answer: I work as an independent contractor through Hilmar ICT Services (KVK 97564303), on an assignment contract per engagement. That contract names the assignment, the scope and the deliverables. I decide myself how the work is carried out, and I invoice monthly on hours worked. There is no employment relationship, and no agency or secondment construction. We settle the wording of the contract before the start, and your own legal people read it with you.

questions.question: How do you handle confidentiality and intellectual property?
questions.answer: Client code stays with the client. The reasoning comes with me, so I can explain any decision on this site in a technical conversation in as much depth as you want. Everything I build in an engagement belongs to the client.

questions.question: What if we turn out not to be a fit?
questions.answer: Then you hear it in the call. If the work sits outside what I do, or the timing does not line up, I say so, and where I can I point at what would fit better.

questions.question: What if the backend cannot change the field in time?
questions.answer: Then the page takes the shape as it is, in one adapter at the edge of the frontend, with a note that says why it is there. The proposal for the source goes to the backend team the same week, so the next version fixes it where it belongs and the adapter comes out.
